Takuan gives Jōtarō money and a Daitokuji seal, orders him to reunite with his father at Shōjuan and travel disguised as priests while avoiding the Kōshū highroad and Nakasendō.

facts.description: Unable to wait for news, Iori rides away from the Hōjō residence intending to find Musashi in Chichibu and discovers the rebuilt Musashino cabin still empty.

Kojirō is now a Hosokawa vassal, with altered formal appearance and a substantial stipend, traveling toward Buzen with the advance party.
Osugi is traveling west with the Hosokawa party to restore family affairs in Mimasaka, recover Gonroku's ashes in Osaka and hold neglected memorial services before resuming her vendetta.
The narration reveals that Osugi has systematically denounced Musashi at Yagyū, Hōjō and government households and has thrown written accusations into official compounds to block his appointment.
Kojirō deliberately tests Iori with his gaze; Iori initially holds steady, showing the effect of Musashi's eye training, though Kojirō later overwhelms him when he tries to throw a stone.
Kojirō writes Musashi a sealed letter as Sasaki Ganryū, Retainer to the House of Hosokawa, inviting a future meeting on the boundary between life and death and makes Iori the messenger.
Shaken by Kojirō's strength, Iori resolves that both he and Musashi must grow stronger and decides to continue toward Chichibu with the letter.
On Musashino Plain Iori unexpectedly reunites with Musashi and Gonnosuke, who have found the wandering Hōjō horse near the Iruma River.
Gonnosuke assures Iori that Musashi's innocence in the Mitsumine theft is now established.
Iori gives Kojirō's sealed challenge letter to Musashi and recounts the Nobidome encounter.
The three spend the night together in the rebuilt Musashino cabin, restoring the teacher-disciple household temporarily.

Kakubei tells Kojirō the bout will occur on Funashima because an island can restrict crowds and intervention.

Kakubei treats marriage to Omitsu as the next step after victory, while Kojirō remains privately aware she could be left behind if he dies.
Kojirō uses solitary falconing with Amayumi to steady himself and draws martial confidence from the bird's predatory focus.
Despite outward confidence, Kojirō increasingly thinks about Omitsu, his dead mother and the possibility of his own death.

facts.description: The Hosokawa government posts the formal order for the thirteenth-day, eight-o'clock Funashima bout and prohibits supporters and civilian boats from approaching.
Matahachi and Akemi reach Kokura as a poor but visibly stable household, traveling with the baby and making a living modestly.
Gempachi recognizes Matahachi from the period when he falsely called himself Sasaki Kojirō; Matahachi now looks back on that impersonation with shame rather than pride.
Gempachi comes from Kōzuke to support Kojirō and recounts the lineage connecting Kojirō to Kanemaki Jisai and the Chūjō tradition.
Kojirō has written two last testaments, one for Kakubei and one for Omitsu, and chooses Tatsunosuke as his allowed attendant.
Kojirō receives the aunt who raised him; she frames the bout as decisive for the honor of the Sasaki family and brings a protective underrobe made by supporters.
Surrounded by admirers and gifts, Kojirō becomes psychologically burdened by the repeated inner command that he must win.
Late news reaches Kojirō's crowded house that Musashi has arrived in the Moji/Kokura area.

facts.description: Musashi crosses from Shimonoseki to Moji to confirm acceptance of the time and place of the bout, but declines to wait for Sado.
Musashi unexpectedly reunites with Iori, gives him serious guidance about education, restraint, life and honorable service, and accepts that the conversation may be their final farewell.
Former Shimmen retainers who knew Munisai find Musashi and invite him to their annual private memorial gathering.
Musashi refuses a public evening at Sado's house because rumors already cast the duel as a factional contest between Sado and Kakubei; he does not want to compromise either man.
The former Shimmen men repeat the horseshoe-making ritual that commemorates poverty after Sekigahara, gratitude to Hosokawa Sansai and loyalty to the vanished Shimmen house.
After the gathering Musashi deliberately keeps out of public view, causing Sado and others to fear he has fled.
When found at Tarōzaemon's house, Musashi refuses Sado's official boat because accepting it could make Sado appear to oppose Tadatoshi; he will use a private Kobayashi boat instead.
Sado allows Iori to accompany him to Funashima on the condition that the boy remain composed even if they must retrieve Musashi's corpse.
Matahachi and Akemi learn from Nuinosuke that Musashi has not fled and take position on a hill from which they hope to watch the distant bout.

chapters.title: The Marriage

source_first_inventory.title: The Marriage
historical_context: Kojirō discards devotional charms to remove psychological obligations
Musashi paints immediately before departure as an expression of selfless concentration

facts.description: Kojirō leaves Kokura for Funashima in Tadatoshi's specially prepared boat with Tatsunosuke and the falcon Amayumi.
Halfway out Kojirō releases Amayumi toward the castle and discards protective charms, including his aunt's underrobe, so that only his 'naked self' remains for the fight.
While others panic over the time, Musashi calmly finishes two paintings and treats the act as discipline in letting a selfless heart act without ego.
Musashi chooses Tarōzaemon's private boat and the secluded Heike Pine departure point to avoid spectacle and factional entanglement.
Osugi apologizes for years of hatred; Musashi forgives her and asks forgiveness for the trouble he caused her, freeing both from the old vendetta.
Musashi and Otsū meet face to face at the Heike Pine after years of separation; Musashi openly admits that apparent coldness did not mean lack of love.
Otsū asks Musashi to say that she is his wife for life; he silently assents and immediately frames the departure in terms of the duty of a samurai's wife and her husband's possible final departure.
After Musashi boards Sasuke's boat, Otsū composes herself, kneels on the beach and sends him away without regrets; Osugi, Gonnosuke and Jōtarō bow with her.

source_first_inventory.title: The Soul of the Deep
historical_context: Final duel occurs around ten o'clock despite the official eight-o'clock appointment
narrator explicitly leaves later revenge-attempt claims unresolved
physical_locations: boat from Shimonoseki through Kanmon strait

facts.description: Musashi travels toward Funashima with the rising/turning tide and is satisfied that the late arrival will place him there around ten.
During the crossing Musashi carves a broken oar into the wooden sword he will use against Kojirō.
Before landing Musashi leaves his long sword in the boat, keeps the short sword at his waist and carries only the oar sword into the duel.

A group of Kojirō supporters has violated Tadatoshi's order and waits near Hikojima with lances, ready to avenge him if he loses; officials remove them from Funashima but do not fully neutralize the risk.
Sado tells Iori to watch the duel as a life lesson, not merely as a display of technique, because Musashi is putting his life on the line before his pupil.
When Kojirō throws away his scabbard, Musashi says he has already lost because he has cast away his future and life, visibly shaking Kojirō.
After multiple exchanges, Kojirō's Drying Pole cuts away Musashi's headband, but Musashi's oar sword strikes and breaks Kojirō's skull.
Kojirō never returns to the living world. Musashi detects a faint trace of breath immediately after the blow and hopes treatment might save him, but the narrator confirms his death.
Musashi feels admiration and gratitude toward Kojirō, judging him the strongest opponent he has faced and recognizing that Kojirō forced him beyond his ordinary limits.
The narration distinguishes Kojirō's confidence in the sword of strength and skill from Musashi's trust in the sword of the spirit.
Musashi bows to Kojirō and the officials, returns to Sasuke's boat and leaves Funashima without administering a coup de grace.
The narration explicitly refuses to certify whether Kojirō's supporters attempted revenge afterward and notes that later criticism of Musashi's conduct persisted.

states.activity: Alive after defeating Kojirō; departs Funashima with Sasuke. Destination and any clash with revenge parties are unrecorded.
